  • Applies when: Applies when requirements mandate customer-controlled keys for Kubernetes secrets in etcd, or an existing KMS configuration must be maintained.

    Low priorityOpen

    The newer KMS data encryption experience for Kubernetes 1.33 or later is currently documented as preview; do not treat it as an unconditional production baseline or assume migration from legacy KMS is automatic. For the selected experience, protect keys with soft delete/purge protection, least-privilege access and tested rotation/recovery. Loss of required keys can make secrets unreadable.

This control establishes Kubernetes compatibility; configure the upgrade mechanism and node-image or OS lifecycle controls separately.

    Kubernetes secrets are encrypted at rest by AKS, but base64 encoding is not encryption and authorized API access can reveal values. Limit synchronization into Kubernetes, restrict secret-read permissions and avoid logging contents. Environment variables require a pod restart to pick up changes and subPath mounts do not receive automatic updates. Key Vault is a secrets management service, not synonymous with a dedicated HSM.

System pools require Linux and VM SKUs with at least 4 vCPUs and 4 GB of memory; B-series and Spot aren't supported. Size above these minima for add-ons, DNS load, failover and surge upgrades, and test that critical pods can reschedule during disruption. Verify actual pod placement, taints and tolerations; the existence of system and user pools alone does not prove separation.

Multi-Tenant - Isolation

0 % Multi-Tenant - Isolation items are ✓

  • Applies when: Shared-cluster deployments with compatible, mutually trusted tenants whose trust, regulatory, lifecycle, and availability requirements permit logical isolation.

    Medium priorityOpen

    Document cluster-scoped resources, operator permissions, noisy-neighbor limits, and platform change ownership. Don't treat separate node pools as a hard security boundary or use logical isolation alone for hostile tenants.

    Related controls

    • Related control 0b56d03c-5fc8-42b1-943b-9e4b4d0f3de8
    • Related control 3b77c0ee-3f84-4a86-bb46-c6dc3070168c

    Documentation

    • Isolating cluster
    • MULTI-TENANCY
  • High priorityOpen

    Namespaces require scoped RBAC, network policy, admission controls, and quotas; implement those controls separately when logical isolation is appropriate. Node pools share the Kubernetes API and are not a hard security boundary. Separate clusters still need independent identity, network, policy, and data-access controls. Regional resilience also requires application traffic routing, data replication, and tested failover; deploying a second cluster alone doesn't provide disaster recovery.

    Related controls

    • Related control 0b56d03c-5fc8-42b1-943b-9e4b4d0f3de8

    Documentation

    • Isolating cluster

  • Applies when: Only estates with multiple AKS clusters that require coordinated update promotion; Fleet is an implementation choice, not a requirement for every cluster.

    High priorityOpen

    Fleet update runs honor member maintenance windows. Choose Latest images for freshness or Consistent images available across participating regions for repeatable testing. Coordinate Fleet with cluster auto-upgrade policies so independent updates don't bypass your intended rollout order. Approval gates, label-based groups, concurrency and failure thresholds, and the SecurityPatch channel are preview features in the current documentation; don't assume all orchestration controls have the same support status.

    Documentation

    • Fleet update orchestration concepts and preview controls
    • Configure Fleet update runs
    • OPERATIONS
    • RESILIENCY

  • Applies when: Only multi-cluster estates evaluating Fleet for a defined update, placement, or governance need; single-cluster deployments and estates without that need are excluded.

    Medium priorityOpen

    Use cluster labels and placement policies deliberately and separate resource deployment from traffic routing and state replication. Supported operations differ by member cluster type. Fleet automated deployments, DNS-based load balancing, and cross-cluster networking are documented as preview; assess their support terms independently rather than treating Fleet as one uniformly GA feature.

Storage

0 % Storage items are ✓
  • High priorityOpen

    Documentation

    • Storage considerations for Azure Kubernetes Service
    • Choose the right storage type
    • STORAGE
  • Medium priorityOpen

    Different types and sizes of nodes are available. Each node (underlying VM) size provides a different amount of core resources such as CPU and memory. These VM sizes have a maximum number of disks that can be attached. Storage performance also varies between VM sizes for the maximum local and attached disk IOPS (input/output operations per second). If your applications require Azure Disks as their storage solution, plan for and choose an appropriate node VM size. The amount of CPU and memory isn't the only factor when you choose a VM size. The storage capabilities are also important.

    Documentation

    • Size the nodes for storage needs
    • STORAGE
  • Low priorityOpen

    Documentation

    • Dynamically provision volumes
    • STORAGE
  • Medium priorityOpen

    Snapshots are generally crash-consistent, not automatically application-consistent or atomic across volumes. Use supported application hooks or database-native backup and recovery to meet consistency needs. Inventory skipped or unsupported volumes, protect external data services separately, and do not install the AKS Backup extension alongside Velero.

    Externalizing state reduces cluster recovery coupling but does not automatically configure replication or protect against deletion and corruption. Set and test each service's backup and failover policies. Stateful workloads can also run on AKS when their storage and operational requirements are explicitly managed.

Networking

0 % Networking items are ✓
  • Medium priorityOpen

    Overlay pods use a separate pod CIDR, and traffic leaving the cluster is translated to node addresses; they are not directly reachable from connected networks. Flat networking uses VNet pod addresses and needs larger subnets. Kubenet retires on March 31, 2028: inventory existing clusters and validate the supported migration to Azure CNI Overlay, including policies, IP ranges, node reimaging and workload disruption, before that date.

    Documentation

    • CNI networking models and data planes
    • Upgrade IPAM and the network data plane
    • Azure CNI Overlay
    • Bring your own CNI
    • Add a node pool with a unique subnet
    • NETWORK
  • High priorityOpen

    Azure CNI Overlay allocates a /24 pod block per node, even when maxPods is smaller. Flat Node Subnet networking reserves pod addresses based on maxPods; Pod Subnet dynamic and static block allocation have different reservation rules. Include simultaneous upgrades and future pools, and monitor address utilization.

    Documentation

    • Plan IP addressing for your cluster
    • NETWORK

Inventory NGINX annotations, snippets, DNS, certificates and private frontend settings; test equivalents and staged cutover. The application routing Gateway API implementation does not support all NGINX capabilities and cannot coexist with the Istio service mesh add-on.

  • Applies when: Applies to multi-region applications requiring global traffic distribution or regional failover.

    Medium priorityOpen

    Configure application-aware health probes and regional origin priorities; measure failover and recovery against RTO under realistic traffic. Traffic Manager answers DNS queries rather than proxying application traffic, so test DNS TTLs and client caching. Front Door provides an HTTP/HTTPS data path; test TLS, private-origin connectivity and connection draining for the chosen design. Consider supported cross-region L4 routing separately when required by protocol. Align routing with data replication and regional capacity: traffic failover neither replicates data nor eliminates detection and recovery delays.

    High priorityOpen

    For supported application routing Gateway API integration, use an unversioned Key Vault certificate URI, a correctly federated service account and least-privilege Key Vault access; use the documented integration for the chosen controller rather than legacy NGINX flags. Test issuance, rotation propagation and listener reload, SAN/hostname matching, certificate chain and client trust, plus backend certificate validation wherever TLS is re-encrypted. Retain externally observed TLS handshake and renewal evidence for the entire intended encrypted path. Application certificate lifecycle is separate from AKS node and cluster CA rotation.

Resource Management

0 % Resource Management items are ✓

  • Applies when: Only Linux burst workloads compatible with Azure Container Instances and the selected virtual-node implementation's networking, storage, identity, and Kubernetes API limitations.

    Low priorityOpen

    Validate the feature matrix for the selected implementation: Virtual Nodes v2 is a preview extension, not the original add-on, and its preview support terms must be acceptable. V2 supports init containers and Azure Files PVCs but requires Azure CNI node-subnet mode and doesn't support Overlay, Cilium, NPM, Windows, BYO VNets, or daemonsets. Account for extension CPU and memory overhead and keep system components on regular AKS nodes.

    Large nodes can improve bin packing but increase the failure blast radius or drain impact; small nodes increase per-node overhead and can leave large pods unschedulable. Record capacity tests showing that large pods fit and enough headroom remains for failover and surge upgrades. Where supported, node auto-provisioning can select VM sizes dynamically, but still depends on accurate pod requests and capacity constraints.

  • High priorityOpen

    CPU limits throttle execution and can harm latency-sensitive workloads even when the node has spare CPU; evaluate them against tenant isolation requirements. Exceeding memory limits can trigger OOM termination, with restart behavior determined by the workload and restart policy, not guaranteed pod relocation.     High priorityOpen

    HPA CPU utilization depends on CPU requests. Review observed CPU, memory, throttling, OOM events, and ephemeral-storage consumption when rightsizing. Start VPA in recommendation mode and account for update-mode disruption before enabling automatic changes. Don't combine automatic VPA changes with HPA scaling on the same CPU or memory metrics; use recommendations or deliberately separate signals such as custom/external metrics. Scaling pods alone doesn't create nodes, and scaling nodes doesn't fix quota, topology, or admission failures.

    High priorityOpen

    When using Azure Backup, Operational backups use snapshots and extension metadata storage in your subscription; eligible Azure Disk backups can also transfer to the Vault tier, but a Backup vault does not mean all backup data is vaulted. Check the live support matrix: Azure Files SMB requires CSI driver 1.32+, is Operational-tier only with at most 30-day retention, and has network, file-count, and restore-location restrictions. NFS Files, Blob CSI, Azure Container Storage, and in-tree PVs are not covered. Enable CSI snapshots, supported managed identities, a healthy Linux backup extension, Trusted Access, and required networking/RBAC; don't co-install Velero with that extension. Snapshot backups are crash-consistent, not automatically application-consistent or atomic across volumes; use supported application hooks or database-native protection when needed. Protect excluded resources and external services separately and validate that source deletion cannot remove the only recovery copy.

    High priorityOpen

    The current matrix describes up to 24-hour primary-region and up to 36-hour secondary-region vaulted RPO, not continuous point-in-time recovery. Vaulting is region-limited and currently supports at most 100 Azure Disk PVs per backup instance with disks no larger than 1 TB, public disk network access enabled, and no Disk Encryption Set or Microsoft Entra data-access authentication. Azure Files is not eligible. Do not weaken required security controls simply to enable vaulting; choose another supported recovery strategy when necessary. Test target-cluster capacity, compatible APIs, identities, networking, recovery order, and cleanup of staged restore resources.

    PDBs constrain voluntary Eviction API operations such as normal node drains, not hardware or zone failures, direct pod deletion, or Deployment and StatefulSet rolling updates. Involuntary disruptions can reduce the remaining disruption allowance but aren't prevented by the budget. A zero-disruption budget can block maintenance; permit at least one eviction where the workload allows it and document coordination when it doesn't. Consider unhealthyPodEvictionPolicy: AlwaysAllow when an unhealthy pod would otherwise block draining, and test that policy against application recovery behavior. A PDB isn't an uptime guarantee.

Reference appendix — unscored

Tools and naming guidance are references, not production controls. They do not affect completion.

  • Customize the name of the MC_ resource group Reference guidance: if naming policy requires it, choose a custom node resource group name when creating the cluster. The name cannot be changed afterward; AKS manages this group's infrastructure regardless of its name. The supported MC_ default is not a readiness deficiency.

    • OPERATIONS
  • Reference: maintained Kubernetes operations tools Reference catalog, not a readiness control: select maintained Kubernetes tools that fit the team's workflows. Review release activity, supply-chain provenance, kubeconfig access and compatibility before adoption; desktop tools and plugins can inherit powerful cluster permissions. No particular tool is required to complete the checklist.
